title: Senses, nerves and reaction time
specPoints: Year 9 bridging: stimulus and response, neurones, the reflex arc and reaction time

tips.title: Sensory towards, motor away
tips.body: **Sensory** neurones carry impulses **towards** the CNS from a receptor; **motor** neurones carry them **away** to an effector. If the question says *from the spinal cord to the muscle*, the word is motor; *from the skin to the spinal cord* is sensory. The **relay** neurone is the link between them, inside the CNS.

tips.title: Seven parts, in order
tips.body: A reflex arc answer is a sequence: **stimulus, receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector, response**. Count seven. The relay neurone is the one most often left out, and swapping sensory and motor loses both marks.

tips.title: Reflex or decision?
tips.body: If it is **fast, automatic and the same every time**, and you could not stop it, it is a **reflex**, coordinated by the spinal cord or, for a few like blinking, the brain stem, with no decision made. If you **chose** it, or could have done something else, the **thinking part of the brain** decided, and that took a reaction time.

tips.title: Read the ruler table, do not calculate
tips.body: The distance a dropped ruler falls converts to reaction time with a table: **20 cm is 0.20 s**, 10 cm is 0.14 s, 30 cm is 0.25 s. Further means slower. The physics behind it is not needed here; the design of the test is.

tips.title: Stimulants shorten, depressants lengthen
tips.body: **Caffeine** is a stimulant: reaction time gets slightly **shorter**. **Alcohol** is a depressant: reaction time gets **longer**, and judgement gets worse at the same time, which is the dangerous combination for a driver.

why.matters: Everything you do that involves the outside world runs through this one chain: something changes, a receptor notices, the nervous system decides or does not bother deciding, and a muscle moves. The chain is fast enough that you never see it working, which is why it takes a topic to notice it. The same chain is what a hot pan, a cricket ball, a driver's phone and a glass of wine all act on, and once you know where the delays are you can predict who catches the ruler and who hits the car in front. It is also the groundwork for the GCSE unit on the nervous system, which adds the structure of a neurone and the gap between one and the next.

examples.title: The hot pan
examples.body: Touch a hot pan and your hand is off it before you know it hurts. The impulse from the skin went to your spinal cord and straight back out to the arm muscles, and only afterwards up to the brain, which is why the pain arrives second. Nobody decided anything, and you could not have chosen to keep your hand there. That is the whole point of a reflex: for a burn, a blow to the eye or a foot on a pin, a fixed fast answer beats a considered one.

visual.alt: A flow chart of the hot-pan reflex: skin, sensory neurone to the spinal cord, relay neurone across with no decision, motor neurone to the arm, the muscle contracts and the pain arrives only afterwards

examples.title: The car in front brakes
examples.body: At 30 mph a car covers about 13 metres every second. The brake lights ahead come on, and for about 0.7 s nothing happens: light reaches the eye, the brain recognises the lights, decides, and sends the impulse to the leg. In that time the car has travelled 9 metres, the thinking distance in the Highway Code. A phone in the hand roughly doubles the reaction time and so doubles that distance. Alcohol lengthens it too, and hides the fact. The physics of stopping starts with the biology of reacting.

props.caption: How far the car travels before the brakes are touched

visual.alt: Two bars to scale: nine metres of thinking distance at thirty miles an hour with a reaction time of 0.7 seconds, and eighteen metres when the reaction time is doubled by a phone

examples.title: The ruler drop in class
examples.body: A partner holds a ruler, drops it without warning, and you catch it. Where your thumb lands says how long you took: catch it at 20 cm and you took a fifth of a second, at 10 cm and you took 0.14 s. The test is so simple that its faults teach the method: a countdown lets you anticipate, a single catch could be luck, and practice during the first set changes the second. Done properly, with repeats and means, it will show whether a coffee, a bad night's sleep or a friend talking to you changes your reaction time.

visual.alt: A table converting the distance a dropped ruler falls into reaction time, from five centimetres and a tenth of a second to thirty centimetres and a quarter of a second

steps.title: Stimulus and response
steps.body:
Living things **detect changes** and **respond** to them. A change that is detected is a **stimulus**: a ball flying at your face, a hot pan, a smell of burning, a word spoken behind you.

**The chain is always the same:**

**stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response**

- The **receptor** detects the stimulus. Receptors are cells, usually gathered in a **sense organ**: light-sensitive cells in the eye, sound-sensitive cells in the ear, touch, pressure, temperature and pain receptors in the skin, chemical receptors in the tongue and nose.
- The **coordinator** decides what to do: the **brain** and **spinal cord**, together the **central nervous system**, or **CNS**.
- The **effector** carries out the response. Effectors are **muscles**, which contract, and **glands**, which release something: sweat, saliva, a hormone.
- The **response** is what happens: you duck, you snatch your hand back, your mouth waters.

**Receptors and effectors are joined to the CNS by nerves**, which carry the messages as tiny **electrical impulses**. The whole system, brain, spinal cord and nerves, is the **nervous system**, and it is fast: the ball is dodged before you have thought about it.

steps.title: Neurones: the wiring
steps.body:
A nerve is a bundle of **neurones**, the cells that carry impulses, and there are three kinds, named for the direction they carry.

- A **sensory neurone** carries the impulse **from a receptor to the CNS**.
- A **relay neurone** sits **inside the CNS** and passes the impulse on, from sensory to motor.
- A **motor neurone** carries the impulse **from the CNS to an effector**.

A neurone is a cell like any other, with a nucleus and a cell body, but it is drawn out into a long thin fibre, the **axon**, that can run from your spinal cord to your toe. The impulse travels along the axon as a wave of **electrical** change. In the fastest neurones, which are wrapped in a fatty insulating sheath, it moves at up to about **120 metres a second**. A sprinter manages about 10. In a tenth of a second the impulse has gone 12 metres and the sprinter one.

**Where one neurone meets the next** there is a tiny gap. The impulse cannot jump it; instead the first neurone releases a chemical that crosses the gap and starts a new impulse in the second. The GCSE unit names this gap and looks at it closely. For now, the point is that the chain is a **relay**, not one wire.

The names are the marks. *Sensory* means towards the CNS; *motor* means away from it, to a muscle. A question that says *the impulse travels from the spinal cord to the muscle* is asking for **motor neurone**.

steps.title: The reflex arc
steps.body:
Touch a hot pan and your hand is off it before you feel the burn. That is a **reflex**: a response that is **fast, automatic, and does not need the brain to decide**. Reflexes protect you from damage, and the pathway they use is the **reflex arc**.

The impulse goes to the **spinal cord** and straight back out, without waiting for the brain:

**stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in the spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector → response**

The brain finds out afterwards, which is why the pain arrives after the hand has already moved. The knee jerk and pulling your foot off a drawing pin work the same way, through the spinal cord. Blinking when something comes at your eye, your pupil shrinking in bright light, and coughing when something goes down the wrong way are reflexes too, but they are coordinated by the **brain stem** instead, the automatic part of the brain: still no decision, and a loop that does not go down to the spine.

**What makes it fast is what it leaves out.** A decision in the brain takes time; the reflex arc uses the shortest possible path and no decision at all. The cost is that you cannot choose not to do it, which is exactly what you want when the alternative is a burn.

In an answer, the arc is a **sequence**, and every link is a mark. Miss out the relay neurone, or put the motor neurone before the sensory one, and the marks go with it.

visuals.alt: A flow chart of the reflex arc for touching a hot pan: skin receptors, sensory neurone to the spinal cord, relay neurone, motor neurone to the arm, biceps contracts and the hand is pulled away

steps.title: Reaction time, and the ruler drop
steps.body:
Most responses are not reflexes. They go through the **brain**, which takes time to notice the stimulus, decide, and send the impulse out. The time from stimulus to response is your **reaction time**, and it is typically between **0.2 s and 0.9 s**, depending on the person, the stimulus and what else they are doing.

**Measuring it with a ruler.** A partner holds a ruler vertically with the zero at the level of your open thumb and finger. Without warning they drop it; you catch it as soon as you see it move. The distance it fell before you caught it tells you the time, because a falling object covers a known distance in a known time. The conversions in the table come from that physics, and you read them off rather than work them out.

**Making it a fair test.** Same hand, same starting gap between finger and thumb, the same partner dropping, no warning and no counting down. **Repeat** five times and take the **mean**, because reaction time varies from catch to catch. Anything you change on purpose, such as talking to the catcher, is the one thing that should differ between runs.

**What changes it.** Reaction time gets **longer** with tiredness, distraction, alcohol and some medicines. It gets **shorter** with practice and with stimulants such as caffeine, though only a little. It is why the drop test is repeated after the catcher has practised, and why a phone in a driver's hand matters so much.

steps.title: Drugs that change the nervous system
steps.body:
Some substances change how fast the nervous system works, and the ruler drop shows it.

- **Stimulants** speed up the nervous system: impulses cross the gaps between neurones more readily, so reaction time gets **shorter**. Caffeine in tea, coffee and energy drinks is the everyday one. The effect is small, and too much causes shaking and a racing heart.
- **Depressants** slow the nervous system down, so reaction time gets **longer**. **Alcohol** is the common one: it also blurs judgement, so a drinker feels sharper as they get slower. That combination is why drink-driving limits exist and why a driver over the limit brakes late.
- Some **medicines** have the same effect as a side effect, which is why hay-fever tablets carry a warning about driving.

**Recreational drugs** cause other harm as well: damage to the liver from alcohol, to the lungs from smoking, and **addiction**, where the body comes to need the drug and stopping causes withdrawal. This is the part of the topic that connects to the GCSE Health unit on lifestyle and disease.

**In an investigation**, a stimulant or depressant is the variable you would change, reaction time is what you would measure, and everything about the drop must stay the same.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Write out the chain from stimulus to response, with all five words.
2. Name the receptor and the sense organ for light, and for chemicals in the air.
3. Which neurone carries an impulse from a receptor to the CNS?

**Part B.**

4. Write the reflex arc for blinking when a fly comes at your eye, naming every part in order.
5. A ruler is caught after falling 15 cm. Use the table to give the reaction time.
6. Give two things that make reaction time longer and one that makes it shorter.

**Part C.**

7. Say why a reflex is faster than a decision to move, and why that is useful.
8. Two students compare reaction times but one uses a warning of "ready, steady, go". Say why this spoils the comparison and how to fix it.
9. A driver has had two glasses of wine. Use reaction time and thinking distance to say why they are more likely to crash.

For question 4, the relay neurone is the link most often forgotten.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Reflex against decision.** A reflex is coordinated by the spinal cord or, for some like blinking, the brain stem, leaving out the **thinking, decision-making** part of the brain, so there is no decision and the path is as short as it can be. A voluntary action goes up to that thinking part, waits for a choice, and comes back down. The reflex is faster for exactly that reason, and it is automatic for the same reason: nothing in the loop can say no. An answer that says *reflexes are fast because they do not involve the brain* is not quite right, since the brain stem runs some reflexes too; the one that says *because the impulse takes the shortest path, through the spinal cord or brain stem, with no decision made* has the marks.

**Why reaction time can never be zero.** Even a reflex takes time: the impulse has to travel along the neurones, cross the gaps between them, and the muscle has to contract. A voluntary response adds the brain's processing on top. So the ruler always falls some distance, and a catch at 0 cm would mean the catcher was guessing.

**Reading the ruler drop properly.** The test measures the time from *seeing the ruler move* to *the fingers closing*. Anything that lets the catcher predict the drop, a countdown, a twitch of the dropper's hand, a fixed rhythm, measures anticipation instead. And a single catch is one sample of a variable quantity: the mean of several catches is the result, and a very short one among long ones is worth a second look.

**Thinking distance is reaction time made visible.** At 30 mph a car covers about 13 metres every second. With a reaction time of 0.7 s that is 9 metres of road before the brakes are even touched, and a phone in the hand can double the reaction time and so double that distance. The Physics course uses these figures for stopping distances; this topic is where the 0.7 s comes from.

**Alcohol is the dangerous case** because it lengthens reaction time *and* dulls the judgement that would notice. A tired driver knows they are tired; a drinker often feels fine.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response.** Receptors are cells in the sense organs; the coordinator is the **CNS** (brain and spinal cord); effectors are **muscles** and **glands**.
- Nerves are bundles of **neurones** carrying **electrical impulses**, at up to about **120 m/s** in the fastest.
- **Sensory** neurones run from a receptor **to** the CNS; **relay** neurones sit inside it; **motor** neurones run from the CNS **to** an effector.
- A **reflex** is fast and automatic: **receptor → sensory → relay (spinal cord) → motor → effector**, with the brain told afterwards.
- **Reaction time** is the delay from stimulus to response, typically **0.2 to 0.9 s**. The ruler drop converts distance fallen to time: **20 cm is 0.20 s**.
- Fair test: same hand and gap, no warning, **repeat and take the mean**.
- **Stimulants** (caffeine) shorten reaction time slightly; **depressants** (alcohol) lengthen it and dull judgement. Tiredness and distraction lengthen it.
- Thinking distance is reaction time on the road: **9 m at 30 mph**, and doubled if reaction time doubles.

questions.prompt: A driver at 30 mph, about 13 m/s, has a reaction time of 0.7 s, giving a thinking distance of 9 m. They pick up a phone and their reaction time doubles. What happens to the thinking distance?

questions.prompt: A person's spinal cord is damaged below the neck. They can still blink when something comes at their eye, but cannot pull their hand from a hot object. Which explanation fits?
questions.solution: Both are reflexes, but they use different parts of the CNS. The blink is coordinated in the **brain stem**, above the injury, so it still works. The hand-withdrawal reflex needs a **relay neurone in the spinal cord** at the level of the arm, below the damage, so the arc is broken.

questions.prompt: A class compares reaction times before and after an energy drink. Which design gives a result you could trust?
questions.solution: Reaction time **varies** from catch to catch, so a single drop each way could differ by chance; **ten drops and the means** show the real change. Everything except the drink must stay the same, including the catcher, or the comparison is not fair. A warning measures anticipation.

questions.prompt: Why is a reflex made automatic rather than left for the brain to decide?
questions.solution: The reflex arc is the **shortest path** with **no decision**, so it is as fast as the nervous system allows, and it always fires. For protection that is the right trade: a decision could arrive too late, or wrongly. The brain still gets the impulse, afterwards, and can override the reflex next time if it must.

markScheme.description: A decision takes time and could be wrong; for a burn or a blow to the eye a fast, fixed response is safer

options: Reflexes are learned in childhood and then forgotten by the brain
A decision takes time and could be wrong; for a burn or a blow to the eye a fast, fixed response is safer
The brain cannot receive impulses from the skin, so the spinal cord has to handle them all
The spinal cord is closer to the muscles than the brain is, so it is the only possible route for the impulse

questions.prompt: A cricketer sees a fast ball coming and moves their head out of the way. Describe the pathway from stimulus to response, and explain why this is not a reflex.
questions.solution:
The **stimulus** is the ball, or more exactly the **light** reflected from it. The **receptors** are the **light-sensitive cells in the retina** at the back of each eye, which turn that light into electrical **impulses**. **Sensory neurones** in the optic nerve carry the impulses to the **central nervous system**, and here the pathway differs from a reflex: the impulses go to the **brain**, which works out where the ball is going and how fast, and decides how to move.

The brain then sends impulses along **motor neurones** to the **effectors**, the **muscles** of the neck and shoulders. They **contract**, and the **response** is the head moving out of the ball's path. So the chain is stimulus, receptor, sensory neurone, brain, motor neurone, effector, response, and it is the brain in the middle that makes this a **voluntary action**.

A **reflex** is different in two ways. Its pathway goes through the **spinal cord**, where a **relay neurone** passes the impulse straight from the sensory neurone to the motor neurone with **no decision** made; and it is **automatic**, the same every time and impossible to stop. Pulling a hand off a hot pan is a reflex: the hand moves before the brain knows.

The cricketer's movement is not like that. It needs a **judgement** about where the ball will be, and the movement chosen depends on that judgement; a different ball gets a different response, and a batter can choose to play the ball instead of ducking. That processing is why the response takes a **reaction time**, typically a few tenths of a second, rather than the shorter, fixed time of a reflex arc. Fast as it looks, it is a decision.

Explains that a reflex runs through the spinal cord with a relay neurone and no decision, and is automatic.
Explains that this response is voluntary: the brain judges the ball's path and chooses the movement, which takes longer and can be varied, so it is not a reflex.

questions.prompt: A student wants to find out whether listening to music lengthens reaction time. Describe a method using the ruler drop, and explain the choices that make the result trustworthy.
questions.solution:
**Method.** The partner holds a ruler vertically with the **zero at the level** of the catcher's open thumb and forefinger. Without any warning they let go, the catcher closes their fingers as soon as they see it move, and the distance the ruler fell is read off at the top of the thumb. The **table** converts that distance to a reaction time: 20 cm is 0.20 s, 10 cm is 0.14 s.

**What changes and what is measured.** The **independent variable** is whether the catcher is listening to music; the **dependent variable** is the reaction time. Everything else stays the same, so that music is the only difference between the two sets of results: the **same catcher** and the same hand, the **same starting gap** between finger and thumb, the same partner dropping the ruler, and the same ruler.

**Avoiding a false result.** The drop must come **without a countdown** and at **random moments**, because a catcher who can predict the drop closes their fingers at the expected instant and the test measures anticipation, not reaction. The two conditions should be run in a mixed order, not all the quiet catches first, or **practice** during the first set would shorten the second set's times regardless of the music.

**Repeats and means.** Reaction time **varies from catch to catch**: the same person might catch at 15 cm and then at 22 cm for no reason. So each condition needs **several drops**, say ten, and the **means** are compared. If the mean with music is clearly longer than the mean without, and the difference is bigger than the spread within each set, the music has lengthened the reaction time. A single drop each way could differ by chance and would show nothing.

markScheme.description: as the criteria

criteria.text: Describes the method: partner holds the ruler with zero at the catcher's open finger and thumb, drops it without warning, and the distance fallen is read and converted to time from the table.
Names the variable changed, music or no music, and the one measured, reaction time.
Keeps everything else the same: the same catcher and hand, the same starting gap, the same dropper, no countdown, and the drops at random moments.
Repeats several drops in each condition and compares the means, and explains why: reaction time varies from catch to catch, and a single drop could differ by chance.

questions.prompt: Light-sensitive cells in the eye and temperature-sensitive cells in the skin are both receptors. What does a receptor do?
questions.solution: A receptor **detects a stimulus**, a change in the surroundings such as light or heat, and starts an **electrical impulse** along a **sensory neurone** towards the central nervous system. Receptors are cells, usually gathered in a **sense organ**: light-sensitive cells in the eye, sound-sensitive cells in the ear, touch, pressure, temperature and pain receptors in the skin, chemical receptors in the tongue and nose. Carrying out the response is the job of an **effector**, a muscle or gland; deciding on the response is the job of the **coordinator**, the brain or spinal cord; and carrying the impulse out to a muscle is the job of a **motor neurone**.

markScheme.description: detects a stimulus and starts an impulse along a sensory neurone

options: Carries out the response, for example by contracting to move part of the body
Decides which response to make, a job that happens in the brain or spinal cord
Carries the impulse out from the spinal cord to a muscle or a gland so that it acts
Detects a stimulus and starts an electrical impulse along a sensory neurone

questions.prompt: Two neurones do not quite touch: there is a tiny gap between them called a synapse. How does the signal get across the gap?
questions.solution: When the electrical impulse reaches the end of the first neurone, a **chemical**, a **neurotransmitter**, is released into the gap. It **diffuses** across and, when it reaches the next neurone, starts a **new electrical impulse** there. So the signal is electrical along a neurone and chemical across a synapse. The chemical step is slower than the electrical one, which is one reason a response through many neurones takes longer than one through few, and it is where **stimulants** and **depressants** act: stimulants make the crossing easier and depressants make it harder. The impulse does not jump as a spark, the fatty sheath around an axon insulates it rather than bridging gaps, and the signal travels one way only.

markScheme.description: a chemical (neurotransmitter) is released, diffuses across the gap and starts a new impulse in the next neurone

options: The electrical impulse jumps across the gap like a spark, in the same way that electricity jumps between two wires that are held close together
The fatty sheath around the first neurone stretches across the gap and carries the impulse into the next neurone like a wire would
A chemical is released from the end of the first neurone, diffuses across the gap and starts a new impulse in the next neurone
The second neurone sends an impulse back towards the first, and the two impulses meet and join together in the middle of the gap

questions.prompt: Caffeine is a stimulant. In a trial, volunteers took the ruler-drop test before a cup of strong coffee and again half an hour after it. Their mean catch distance fell from 18 cm to 14 cm. Which statement interprets the result correctly?
questions.solution: A **stimulant speeds up the nervous system**: impulses cross the gaps between neurones more readily, so the time from seeing the ruler move (the stimulus) to the fingers closing (the response) is **shorter**. In the ruler-drop test a shorter reaction time means the ruler **falls less far** before it is caught, so the fall from 18 cm to 14 cm shows a shorter reaction time, not a longer one. A falling ruler accelerates at the same rate whoever drops it, so it did not fall more slowly; the ruler is always dropped from the same place, with the zero level with the catcher's fingers; and the change is in the nervous system, which is what a stimulant acts on, not in the weight of the hand.

markScheme.description: the stimulant sped up the nervous system, so reaction time shortened and the ruler fell less far

options: The caffeine lengthened reaction time, because a smaller catch distance shows that the volunteers took longer to close their fingers on the ruler
The caffeine made the volunteers' hands lighter and quicker to close, which is a change in the muscles of the hand rather than anywhere in the nervous system
The ruler fell more slowly after the coffee, because the alert volunteers made their partner drop it from a smaller height above their fingers each time
The caffeine sped up the passage of impulses through the nervous system, so reaction time shortened and the ruler fell less far before it was caught

questions.prompt: A penalty kick reaches the goal line about 0.4 s after it is struck. A goalkeeper's reaction time is about 0.2 s, and the dive itself takes about 0.5 s. Which statement explains why goalkeepers so often dive before the ball is kicked?
questions.skill: reaction time in a real situation
questions.solution: If the keeper waited for the kick, the **stimulus** would be the ball leaving the foot. Add the **reaction time** of 0.2 s, the delay before the muscles begin to respond, to the 0.5 s the dive takes, and the keeper would arrive $0.2 + 0.5 = 0.7$ s after the kick, when the ball has been over the line for 0.3 s. Reacting to the kick itself is too slow, so keepers respond to **earlier stimuli**: the angle of the kicker's run-up, their hips and their planted foot. The dive is a decision made in the brain, not a reflex set off by a whistle; diving early does not make reaction time zero, it changes what the stimulus is; and light reaches the keeper's eyes in a tiny fraction of a second, so the keeper sees the kick almost as it happens.

markScheme.description: reaction time plus the dive, 0.7 s, is longer than the ball's 0.4 s, so the keeper must respond to earlier stimuli such as the run-up

options: The dive is a reflex triggered automatically by the sound of the referee's whistle, so it begins before the kick whether the keeper has chosen to move or not
Diving early cuts the keeper's reaction time to zero, so the whole 0.5 s dive is completed inside the 0.4 s before the ball reaches the goal line
Light from the ball takes longer than 0.4 s to reach the keeper's eyes, so the keeper never sees the kick until the ball has already crossed the goal line
Reacting to the kick would take 0.2 s + 0.5 s = 0.7 s, longer than the ball's 0.4 s, so the keeper must respond to earlier stimuli, such as the kicker's run-up

questions.prompt: Name the type of neurone that lies inside the spinal cord and passes the impulse from a sensory neurone to a motor neurone in a reflex arc.
questions.solution: A **relay neurone**. It sits inside the central nervous system, in the spinal cord for a reflex such as pulling a hand from a hot pan, and links the **sensory neurone** coming in from the receptor to the **motor neurone** going out to the effector. Because the link is made in the spinal cord, the response happens before the brain has been told.

markScheme.description: relay neurone

questions.prompt: In the ruler-drop test, a student catches the ruler after it has fallen 14 cm, 19 cm, 16 cm, 17 cm and 19 cm. Calculate the mean distance fallen, in cm.
questions.solution: Add the five readings: $14 + 19 + 16 + 17 + 19 = 85$ cm. Divide by the number of readings: $\dfrac{85}{5} = 17$ cm. Reaction time varies from catch to catch, which is why the test is repeated and the mean is used rather than any single catch. A mean of 17 cm corresponds to a reaction time of a little under 0.2 s.

markScheme.description: adds the five readings to 85 and divides by 5
17 cm

questions.prompt: Reaction time can be worked out from how far a dropped ruler falls before it is caught. The time $t$, in seconds, for the ruler to fall a distance $d$, in metres, is $t = \sqrt{2d \div g}$, where $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$. A volunteer catches the ruler after it has fallen 20 cm. After two alcoholic drinks, the same volunteer catches it after it has fallen 45 cm. Calculate the increase in the volunteer's reaction time, in seconds.
questions.skill: reaction time from the distance fallen
questions.solution: The distances are in centimetres and the formula needs metres, so convert first: 20 cm is 0.20 m and 45 cm is 0.45 m. Before the drinks: $t = \sqrt{2 \times 0.20 \div 10} = \sqrt{0.04} = 0.2$ s. After the drinks: $t = \sqrt{2 \times 0.45 \div 10} = \sqrt{0.09} = 0.3$ s. The increase is $0.3 - 0.2 = 0.1$ s. The ruler-drop table gives the same figures: 20 cm is 0.20 s. Alcohol is a **depressant**, which slows the nervous system and lengthens reaction time; that extra tenth of a second is why a car travelling at 13 m/s goes a further 1.3 m before the driver even begins to brake. Putting 20 and 45 into the formula without converting gives 2 s and 3 s, far longer than any human reaction time, which is the sign that the units were missed.

markScheme.description: converts both distances to metres and substitutes into the formula
reaction times of 0.2 s and 0.3 s

questions.prompt: A person smells smoke in the kitchen and walks out of the room. Describe what happens at each stage of the chain from stimulus to response.
questions.solution: The smoke is the stimulus. Chemical receptors in the nose detect it and send electrical impulses along a sensory neurone to the brain, the coordinator, which is part of the central nervous system. The brain decides to leave and sends impulses along motor neurones to the leg muscles, the effectors, which contract so that the person walks out of the room, the response.

markScheme.description: chemical receptors in the nose detect the smoke (the stimulus) and send impulses along a sensory neurone to the brain, the coordinator
the brain sends impulses along motor neurones to the leg muscles (the effectors), which contract so the person walks out (the response)

criteria.text: States that the smoke is the stimulus, that chemical receptors in the nose detect it, and that impulses pass along a sensory neurone to the brain, the coordinator in the central nervous system
States that the brain sends impulses along motor neurones to the leg muscles, the effectors, which contract so that the person walks out, the response

questions.modelAnswer: The smoke in the air is the stimulus. Chemical receptors in the nose detect it and start electrical impulses, which travel along a sensory neurone to the brain. The brain is the coordinator, part of the central nervous system: it works out what the smell means and decides on a response. It then sends impulses along motor neurones to the effectors, in this case the muscles of the legs, which contract so that the person walks out of the room. Walking out is the response. The whole chain is stimulus, receptor, coordinator, effector, response, and because it passes through the brain it is a decision rather than a reflex.

questions.prompt: In a sprint race the runners start when they hear the starting gun. Electronic starting blocks record how long after the gun each runner begins to push. A start less than 0.1 s after the gun is counted as a false start, even though the runner moved after the gun was fired. Explain why a start that quick is treated as a false start.
questions.skill: why reaction time has a lower limit
questions.solution: The sound of the gun is the stimulus. Receptors in the ear send impulses along sensory neurones to the brain, which has to process the sound and then send impulses along motor neurones to the leg muscles, which then contract. Each stage takes time: the impulse travels along the neurones at a finite speed, crosses the gaps between them by a chemical, and the muscles take time to contract. For this pathway the total is at least about 0.1 s in any human, so reaction time can never be zero. A runner who pushes off in less than 0.1 s therefore cannot have reacted to the gun; they must have anticipated it and started on a guess, which is why the start counts as false even though it came after the gun.

markScheme.description: the pathway: receptors in the ear, sensory neurones to the brain, processing, motor neurones to the leg muscles, which contract
each stage takes time (impulses travel at a finite speed, cross gaps between neurones, muscles take time to contract), so there is a minimum reaction time of about 0.1 s and it can never be zero
a start under 0.1 s cannot be a reaction to the gun, so the runner must have anticipated it and started on a guess

criteria.text: Describes the pathway: the gun is the stimulus, receptors in the ear send impulses along sensory neurones to the brain, which processes the sound and sends impulses along motor neurones to the leg muscles, which contract

Explains that every stage takes time, because impulses travel at a finite speed, cross the gaps between neurones by a chemical and the muscles take time to contract, so the shortest possible reaction time is about 0.1 s and it can never be zero
Concludes that a start in less than 0.1 s cannot be a reaction to the gun, so the runner must have anticipated it and started on a guess, which is why it counts as a false start

questions.modelAnswer:
The sound of the gun is the stimulus. Sound-sensitive receptors in the ear detect it and send electrical impulses along sensory neurones to the brain. The brain has to process the sound, recognise it as the gun and decide to go, and then send impulses along motor neurones down to the leg muscles, which are the effectors. Only when the muscles contract does the runner begin to push against the blocks.

None of these stages is instant. The impulses travel along the neurones at a finite speed, they cross the gaps between neurones by a chemical that has to diffuse across, the brain's processing takes time, and the muscles take time to contract once the impulse arrives. Added together, the shortest reaction time a human can manage for this pathway is about 0.1 s. Practice can bring a runner close to that limit but cannot remove it, because the impulse still has the same distance to travel and the same gaps to cross.

So if the blocks record a push less than 0.1 s after the gun, the runner cannot have been reacting to the sound: there was not time for the impulse to get from the ear to the leg. They must have anticipated the gun and started on a guess that happened to fall just after it. The rule treats that as a false start because the runner did not respond to the stimulus at all.

questions.prompt: A student wants to know whether people react more slowly with the hand they do not write with. Using the ruler-drop test, the student tests their own right hand, the hand they write with, five times and then their left hand five times. Right hand: 15, 17, 16, 18 and 14 cm. Left hand: 20, 22, 48, 19 and 21 cm. The student concludes: "Everybody reacts more slowly with the hand they do not write with." Evaluate the student's method and conclusion, and describe how the investigation could be improved.
questions.solution: The 48 cm catch is anomalous: it is more than twice the other left-hand readings, so the student was probably distracted or missed the ruler, and it should be left out and the drop repeated. Without it the left-hand mean is 20.5 cm against a right-hand mean of 16 cm; with it the left-hand mean is 26 cm, which exaggerates the gap. Both means are distances, but the conclusion is about reaction time, so the distances should be converted to times with the ruler-drop table, and because time rises more slowly than distance the gap in reaction time is smaller than the gap in distance suggests. Even so, the data do support a slower left hand, but only for this one student. A sample of one cannot justify a claim about everybody; the student should test many people, including some who write with their left hand. The method also needs the same conditions for both hands: the same partner dropping with no warning, the zero of the ruler level with the fingers each time, and the same starting gap. Testing the right hand first and then the left means practice or tiredness could differ between the hands, so the order should be alternated, with a few practice drops first and more repeats of each hand.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points, such as noticing the 48 cm reading or saying that more people should be tested, with little use of the data and no clear judgement on the conclusion

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): uses the data, treating 48 cm as anomalous and comparing the means, and judges the conclusion, but with a gap such as no comment on the sample of one, no conversion of distance to time, or no improvement to how the drops are carried out

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): handles the anomaly and compares means with it removed, converts distance to reaction time, judges that the data support a slower non-writing hand for this student only, and gives linked improvements: many students, more repeats, the same drop conditions for both hands and an alternated order

criteria.text: Identifies the 48 cm catch as anomalous, far from the other left-hand readings, and says it should be left out of the mean and the drop repeated
Compares the means with the anomaly removed: right hand 16 cm, left hand 20.5 cm (26 cm if the 48 cm is kept, which exaggerates the gap), so the data do show a slower left hand for this student

Points out that the conclusion is about reaction time, so the distances should be converted to times, using the ruler-drop table or t = √(2d ÷ g); the gap in time is then smaller than the gap in distance suggests
Judges that a sample of one student cannot support a claim about everybody; many students should be tested, including some who write with their left hand
Describes control of the drop: the same partner dropping with no warning or countdown, the zero of the ruler level with the fingers, the same starting gap between finger and thumb, for both hands

Notes that testing the right hand first and then the left lets practice or tiredness differ between the hands, so the order should be alternated, with practice drops first and more repeats of each hand

questions.modelAnswer:
**The data.** The 48 cm catch with the left hand is anomalous: the other four left-hand readings lie between 19 and 22 cm, and 48 cm is more than twice any of them. The student was probably distracted or fumbled the catch. It should be left out and that drop repeated. With it included, the left-hand mean is $130 \div 5 = 26$ cm, which makes the left hand look far slower than it is; without it, the mean of the remaining four readings is $82 \div 4 = 20.5$ cm. The right-hand mean is $80 \div 5 = 16$ cm, from five readings that are close together.

The conclusion is about reaction time, but the student has compared distances. The distances should be converted to times with the ruler-drop table. Because the ruler speeds up as it falls, time rises more slowly than distance, so the gap between 16 cm and 20.5 cm is a smaller gap in reaction time than the distances suggest. Even so, every left-hand reading is longer than every right-hand reading, so the data do support a slower reaction with the left hand for this student.

**The conclusion.** The claim is about everybody, but only one person was tested, and only one who writes with the right hand. A sample of one cannot show what is true of people in general, and it says nothing about people who write with their left hand. The conclusion should be limited to this student until many more people have been tested.

**The method.** For the comparison to be fair, everything except the hand must stay the same: the same partner dropping the ruler without warning or a countdown, the zero mark level with the fingers at the start, and the same gap between finger and thumb for both hands. The order matters too. The right hand was tested first, so by the time the left hand was tested the student had either practised, flattering the left hand, or tired, which would make it look worse. The order should be alternated between students, with a few unrecorded practice drops first.

**Improvements.** Test the whole class, right- and left-handed writers alike, with ten drops per hand, repeating any anomalous catch; alternate which hand goes first; convert each mean distance to a reaction time; and only then compare the two hands.

examTechnique.body:
The marks here are for **order and direction**. A reflex arc answer is a list of seven parts in sequence, and the examiner ticks each one; sensory before motor, and the relay neurone in the middle. Direction words matter: *towards* the CNS for sensory, *away* for motor.

The second kind of question is the investigation. For the ruler drop, know the **design** rather than the physics: what is changed, what is measured, what is kept the same, why there is no warning, and why repeats and means are needed. *Explain why this is a reflex* wants two things: coordinated by the **spinal cord or brain stem, with no decision**, and **automatic**, the same every time. *Explain why it is not a reflex* wants the **thinking part of the brain** and a choice.
examinerErrors: Leaving out the **relay neurone**, or putting the motor neurone before the sensory one.
Calling the sense organ the receptor. The **receptor is a cell**: light-sensitive cells in the retina, not *the eye*.

Saying a reflex *does not use the nervous system*, or that *reflexes never involve the brain*: some, such as blinking, are coordinated by the **brain stem**. What every reflex bypasses is **decision-making**, not the whole brain.
Writing that the effector is a nerve. Effectors are **muscles** and **glands**.
Giving one ruler catch each as a comparison, or allowing a countdown, in a method question.
Saying caffeine is a depressant or alcohol a stimulant. **Stimulants shorten** reaction time; **depressants lengthen** it.
Confusing reaction time with the reflex: a reflex is faster than a reaction *because* it makes no decision.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer writes the arc as seven parts in order without prompting and names the direction of each neurone. Asked why a reflex is fast, it says the impulse takes the **shortest path, through the spinal cord or brain stem, and no decision is made**, and it can say what that costs: the response cannot be stopped. Asked whether a movement is a reflex, it looks for a **choice** and answers accordingly. Given the ruler drop it designs the test as an investigation: the variable changed, the one measured, everything held constant, no warning, several drops and the means compared, and it can say what a single suspiciously short catch means. And it connects the 0.7 s of a driver's reaction to the **9 metres** of thinking distance the Physics course uses, and doubles both when a phone appears.
